nodes.label: Behavioral Welfare Economics
nodes.description: How to evaluate welfare when individual choices may not reflect true preferences. The Bernheim-Rangel "beyond revealed preference" framework provides foundations for behavioral welfare economics without assuming choices are utility-maximizing.

nodes.label: Beyond Revealed Preference
key_concepts: Choice process data as auxiliary information

nodes.label: Corrective Taxation & Policy
nodes.description: Optimal design of taxes and regulations when agents have biases. Extends Pigouvian taxation to internalities — self-imposed harms from present bias, inattention, or misperceptions — in addition to externalities.

nodes.label: Distributional Concerns
key_concepts: Optimal soda tax with income heterogeneity

nodes.label: Nudges & Default Effects
nodes.description: Behavioral interventions that alter choice architecture without restricting options. Libertarian paternalism: preserve choice freedom while steering people toward better outcomes through defaults, framing, and social norms.

nodes.label: Sludge & Administrative Burden
nodes.description: Frictions in accessing public programs. Complexity, stigma, and psychological costs reduce take-up of beneficial programs, imposing welfare costs on eligible non-participants.

nodes.label: Present Bias & Self-Control
nodes.description: Time-inconsistent preferences and their policy implications. The β-δ quasi-hyperbolic discounting model captures present focus that distorts savings, health, and labor supply decisions.

nodes.label: Earnings & Labor Policy
nodes.description: Behavioral dimensions of income taxation, labor supply, and social insurance. Covers tax misperceptions, biased beliefs about unemployment, and behavioral hazard in health insurance.

nodes.label: Income Tax Misperceptions
key_concepts: Optimal income tax with behavioral agents

nodes.label: Empirical Methods
nodes.description: Methods for measuring biases and evaluating behavioral interventions in public economics contexts. Bridges structural and reduced-form traditions.

nodes.label: Behavioral Insurance & Social Insurance
nodes.description: How behavioral frictions — inertia, inattention, biased beliefs, adverse selection — shape insurance markets and social insurance programs. Covers health insurance choice, unemployment insurance design, and the welfare cost of behavioral frictions in insurance markets.

nodes.label: Adverse Selection & Inertia
key_concepts: High-deductible plans and blunt cost-sharing responses

nodes.label: Household Finance & Consumer Credit
nodes.description: Behavioral dimensions of household financial decisions: credit card debt, payday lending, liquidity constraints, and intertemporal choice in consumer finance. Connects present-bias theory to real-world debt and savings behavior.

nodes.label: Behavioral Industrial Organization
nodes.description: How firm strategies exploit consumer biases: shrouded add-on prices, overconfidence, switching costs, and inattention in product markets. Covers policy interventions in markets with behavioral consumers.

nodes.label: Inequality, Mobility & Opportunity
nodes.description: Behavioral and structural barriers to economic mobility. How neighborhood effects, information frictions, and administrative barriers prevent low-income households from accessing opportunity.

nodes.label: Beyond Revealed Preference: Choice-Theoretic Foundations for Behavioral Welfare Economics
nodes.summary: Proposes the Bernheim-Rangel framework for welfare analysis without relying on revealed preference. Introduces the unambiguous choice relation P* as the unique welfare criterion satisfying three basic properties. Foundation of modern behavioral welfare economics.

nodes.label: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: A Unified Approach to Behavioral Welfare Economics
nodes.summary: Refines the Bernheim-Rangel framework. Distinguishes direct vs. indirect judgments, argues that behavioral economics challenges indirect but not direct judgments. Provides revised premises for choice-oriented welfare analysis.

nodes.label: Behavioral Economics and Public Policy: A Pragmatic Perspective
nodes.summary: Advocates for the sufficient statistics approach: use reduced-form estimates of behavioral wedges to evaluate policy without fully specifying cognitive models. Frames decision utility vs. experienced utility as alternative welfare foundations.

nodes.label: Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting
nodes.summary: Popularizes the β-δ (quasi-hyperbolic discounting) model. Shows that illiquid assets serve as commitment devices for present-biased consumers. Foundational paper for the self-control literature in behavioral economics.

nodes.label: Temptation and Self-Control
nodes.summary: Axiomatizes temptation preferences where consumers experience a penalty when choosing anything other than the most tempting option. Accounts for choice reversals without time inconsistency.

nodes.label: Evaluating Behaviorally-Motivated Policy: Experimental Evidence from the Lightbulb Market
nodes.summary: Within-subject experiment on lightbulb purchases. Debiasing intervention reveals consumer undervaluation of energy costs. Derives price-metric bias γ and computes optimal corrective subsidy using the internality framework.

nodes.label: Is Addiction 'Rational'? Theory and Evidence
nodes.summary: Incorporates quasi-hyperbolic discounting into the rational addiction model. Derives optimal cigarette tax that corrects both externalities and internalities from self-control failures. Key application of the modified Pigouvian principle.

nodes.label: Tax Incidence when Individuals are Time-Inconsistent: the Case of Cigarette Excise Taxes
nodes.summary: Shows that cigarette taxes can be welfare-improving even for low-income consumers when present bias is sufficiently severe and demand is elastic. Addresses the regressivity concern for sin taxes.

nodes.label: Regressive Sin Taxes, with an Application to the Optimal Soda Tax
nodes.summary: Estimates optimal soda tax accounting for both internalities and externalities. Develops framework for optimal tax when sin goods are regressively consumed. Finds moderate tax justified despite regressivity when corrective benefits dominate.

nodes.label: Optimal Sin Taxes
nodes.summary: Studies taxation of unhealthy foods under present-bias. Shows optimal tax is positive whenever present focus causes overconsumption and consumers are price-sensitive. General application of the modified Pigouvian principle.

nodes.label: Energy Policy with Externalities and Internalities
nodes.summary: Studies optimal policy mix (energy tax + appliance subsidy) when consumers underweight future energy costs. Key result: optimal energy tax is below the Pigouvian level because standard consumers over-respond to it.

nodes.label: Optimal Taxation with Behavioral Agents
nodes.summary: General framework for optimal taxation with behavioral agents. Derives formulas for both commodity and income taxes that generalize standard sufficient statistics by adding price-metric bias terms. Shows Ramsey-style formulas re-emerge with non-salient commodity taxes.

nodes.label: Addiction and Cue-triggered Decision Processes
nodes.summary: Models addiction as cue-triggered hot states. Argues welfare-relevant domain excludes choices made in triggered states using neurobiological evidence. Derives the surprising result that optimal tax on addictive goods may be negative.

nodes.label: Salience and Taxation: Theory and Evidence
nodes.summary: Field experiment + natural experiment showing consumers underreact to taxes not included in posted prices (σ ≈ 0.06–0.35). Derives efficiency cost formula showing underreaction reduces deadweight loss through two channels.

nodes.label: E-ZTAX: Tax Salience and Tax Rates
nodes.summary: Electronic toll collection (E-ZPass) reduces tax salience, leading governments to raise toll rates. Natural experiment showing that salience affects the political economy of taxation.

nodes.label: Libertarian Paternalism
nodes.summary: Introduces libertarian paternalism: preserving choice while steering people toward better outcomes through defaults and framing. Argues planners inevitably influence choices through defaults, so should do so in welfare-enhancing ways.

nodes.label: The Short-Run and Long-Run Effects of Behavioral Interventions: Experimental Evidence from Energy Conservation
nodes.summary: Evaluates Opower social comparison nudges for energy conservation. Finds effects persist but decay over time. Estimates welfare effects of the nudge using willingness-to-pay elicitation.

nodes.label: The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation and Savings Behavior
nodes.summary: Seminal paper documenting dramatic default effects in 401(k) enrollment. Auto- enrollment increases participation rates from ~49% to ~86%. First rigorous evidence of status quo bias in retirement savings.

nodes.label: Optimal Defaults and Active Decisions
nodes.summary: Derives optimal 401(k) default contribution rate. Under long-run welfare criterion, sufficiently low β justifies active choice requirements rather than passive defaults. Shows opt-out maximization can be welfare-improving.

nodes.label: The Welfare Economics of Default Options in 401(k) Plans
nodes.summary: Applies Bernheim-Rangel framework to 401(k) defaults. Shows EVA and EVB bounds on welfare effects lead to similar optimal defaults for contribution rates below 20%. Default is generally insensitive to the decision frame in this range.

nodes.label: Tying Odysseus to the Mast: Evidence from a Commitment Savings Product in the Philippines
nodes.summary: RCT of commitment savings account (SEED) in Philippines. Documents demand for commitment devices, particularly among present-biased individuals. Balance increased 82% relative to control group.

nodes.label: Poverty and Self-Control
nodes.summary: Formalizes internal self-control through history-dependent equilibria. Shows external commitments can undermine internal self-regulation. Low initial assets trap people in poverty by limiting self-control strategies.

nodes.label: Psychological Frictions and the Incomplete Take-Up of Social Benefits
nodes.summary: Field experiment on EITC take-up. Simplified notices dramatically increase take-up. Psychological frictions—not stigma—are the main barrier. Addresses the incomplete take-up puzzle for redistributive programs.

nodes.label: Taxpayer Confusion: Evidence from the Child Tax Credit
nodes.summary: RD design showing taxpayers confuse lump-sum transfers with marginal tax changes. Loss of CTC associated with decline in reported wage income, even though CTC is lump-sum and should not affect labor supply incentives.

nodes.label: Behavioral Hazard in Health Insurance
nodes.summary: Derives optimal copay formula for health insurance with behavioral consumers. Biases can cause over-use of some medications and under-use of others. Extends behavioral public economics framework to health insurance design.

nodes.label: Unemployed but Optimistic: Optimal Insurance Design with Biased Beliefs
nodes.summary: Modifies Baily-Chetty optimal unemployment insurance formula for biased beliefs about reemployment prospects. Slope effect (return to search) vs. level effect (job-finding probability) have different policy implications.

nodes.label: Do Pharmacists Buy Bayer? Informed Shoppers and the Brand Premium
nodes.summary: Pharmacists and doctors buy generic drugs more than laypeople. Uses expert choices as rational consumer benchmark to measure bias from imperfect information. Application of the rational consumer benchmark welfare method.

nodes.label: A Method for Evaluating the Quality of Financial Decision Making
nodes.summary: Introduces financial competence measure based on WTA discrepancies for equivalent claims. Shows standard financial education increases tested knowledge but not decision quality—motivational rhetoric drives behavioral change, not substance.

nodes.label: Ramsey Strikes Back: Optimal Commodity Taxes and Redistribution in the Presence of Salience Effects
nodes.summary: Shows Atkinson-Stiglitz theorem breaks down with non-salient commodity taxes. Optimal commodity taxes follow Diamond (1975) Many-person Ramsey rule. Differential commodity taxes become useful even when income taxation is available.

nodes.label: Psychology and Economics: Evidence from the Field
nodes.summary: Comprehensive survey of field evidence on behavioral economics: limited attention, non-standard beliefs, and non-standard preferences. Organizes findings around deviations from the standard model and evaluates their policy implications. Gateway reference for the field.

nodes.label: Attention Variation and Welfare: Theory and Evidence from a Tax Salience Experiment
nodes.summary: ★ STARRED. Runs a tax salience experiment with heterogeneous attention. Shows that attention to taxes varies substantially across consumers, and that ignoring this heterogeneity biases welfare calculations. Derives optimal tax formula accounting for attention variation.

nodes.label: Understanding Tax Policy: How Do People Reason?
nodes.summary: ★ STARRED. Uses large-scale survey experiments to study how people reason about tax policy. Finds respondents use "mental frameworks" that shape policy views independently of standard economic logic. Provides new approach to measuring policy perceptions at scale.

nodes.label: Save More Tomorrow™: Using Behavioral Economics to Increase Employee Saving
nodes.summary: Introduces the SMarT (Save More Tomorrow) program: employees commit in advance to automatically increase their 401(k) contribution with each pay raise. Exploits present bias and inertia. Participation rates triple relative to control. Highly influential in policy design.

nodes.label: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts
nodes.summary: Uses Danish administrative data to show 401(k) contributions from automatic employer contributions do not crowd out active saving, while subsidies primarily shift saving across accounts. 85% of people are "passive savers." Implications for optimal retirement savings policy design.

nodes.label: RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudges Units
nodes.summary: Analyzes 126 RCTs run by two large government nudge units. Academic-published nudges have 8× larger effect sizes than unpublished trials — publication bias explains much of the "nudge optimism." Provides calibration for real-world effectiveness of behavioral interventions at scale.

nodes.label: The Welfare Effects of Nudges: A Case Study of Energy Use Social Comparisons
nodes.summary: Combines Opower energy nudge data with willingness-to-pay elicitation to compute welfare effects. Finds the nudge is welfare-improving but imprecisely targeted: it helps the unbiased as well as the biased, and the WTP for the nudge is on average positive but heterogeneous.

nodes.label: Revealed Preference Analysis with Framing Effects
nodes.summary: Extends revealed preference welfare analysis to account for framing effects. Introduces the concept of "frame-invariant preferences" and characterizes when observed choices identify welfare even in the presence of framing. Bridges the Bernheim-Rangel framework and revealed preference.

nodes.label: Measuring the Welfare Effects of Shame and Pride
nodes.summary: Develops a method to measure the welfare effects of social image concerns (shame and pride) in behavioral interventions. Uses a within-subject design to elicit WTP for avoiding shame from charitable giving. Shows shame and pride have substantial and heterogeneous welfare effects that standard analyses miss.

nodes.label: Equilibrium Effects of Food Labeling Policies
nodes.summary: Studies Chile's mandatory warning labels on unhealthy foods (the "black octagon" policy). Combines scanner data with a structural model to identify equilibrium effects including firm reformulation responses. Labels reduce unhealthy purchases and trigger substantial product reformulation.

nodes.label: Choice in Insurance Markets: A Pigouvian Approach to Social Insurance Design
nodes.summary: ★ STARRED. Develops a Pigouvian framework for social insurance that accounts for behavioral frictions in insurance choice. Distinguishes between private and social valuations of insurance. Shows corrective subsidies are welfare-improving when behavioral frictions cause under-insurance.

nodes.label: Moral Hazard versus Liquidity and Optimal Unemployment Insurance
nodes.summary: Disentangles moral hazard from liquidity effects in unemployment insurance. Shows that most of the consumption-smoothing benefit of UI comes from liquidity, not moral hazard reduction. Implication: optimal UI is higher than traditional models suggest.

nodes.label: Reference-Dependent Job Search: Evidence from Hungary
nodes.summary: Uses administrative data from Hungary to show job search effort and re-employment hazard follow reference-dependent patterns. A spike at UI benefit exhaustion is consistent with loss aversion around a reference wage. Structurally estimates a reference-dependent job search model.

nodes.label: Adverse Selection and Inertia in Health Insurance Markets: When Nudging Hurts
nodes.summary: ★ Boot camp key paper. Documents large inertia in health insurance plan choice. Reduced-form and structural evidence that inertia generates adverse selection: inertia keeps healthy individuals in generous plans. Eliminating inertia reduces welfare through adverse selection even as it improves choice quality.

nodes.label: Health Insurance for 'Humans': Information Frictions, Plan Choice, and Consumer Welfare
nodes.summary: ★ Boot camp key paper. Combines revealed preference data with a survey on plan knowledge to separate information frictions from risk preferences in health insurance choice. Shows that information frictions explain much of the apparent risk aversion. Information provision substantially improves welfare.

nodes.label: Choice Inconsistencies among the Elderly: Evidence from Plan Choice in the Medicare Part D Program
nodes.summary: Reveals systematic choice inconsistencies in Medicare Part D drug plan selection. Enrollees overweight premiums relative to expected out-of-pocket costs and exhibit status quo bias. Implies substantial welfare losses from suboptimal plan choice among the elderly.

nodes.label: Choose to Lose: Health Plan Choices from a Menu with Dominated Options
nodes.summary: Shows 61% of employees choose dominated health insurance plans. The magnitude of welfare losses is large (hundreds to thousands of dollars). Employees with more education and actuarial training make significantly better choices. Motivates simplification of health insurance menus.

nodes.label: The Social Determinants of Choice Quality: Evidence from Health Insurance in the Netherlands
nodes.summary: ★ STARRED. Examines how socioeconomic factors predict health insurance choice quality using Dutch administrative data. Lower-income, less-educated households make systematically worse plan choices. Social determinants of choice quality have strong implications for corrective insurance policy design.

nodes.label: Creating Moves to Opportunity: Experimental Evidence on Barriers to Neighborhood Choice
nodes.summary: ★ STARRED. RCT offering housing search assistance + financial support to voucher-holding families in Seattle. Creates Moves to Opportunity (CMTO) treatment triples the share of families moving to high-opportunity neighborhoods. Shows behavioral barriers — search frictions, limited information — are the key obstacle, not preferences.

nodes.label: Behavioral Household Finance
nodes.summary: ★ STARRED. Comprehensive handbook chapter reviewing the behavioral household finance literature. Covers retirement savings, consumer credit, mortgage decisions, and wealth accumulation. Synthesizes findings on present bias, inertia, and limited attention in household financial decisions.

nodes.label: Regulating Consumer Financial Products: Evidence from Credit Cards
nodes.summary: Evaluates the CARD Act of 2009 (credit card regulation) using a regression discontinuity design. Finds the Act reduced fees by $11.9 billion per year with minimal offsetting increases in interest rates. Provides causal evidence that consumer financial protection regulation can improve welfare.

nodes.label: Are High-Interest Loans Predatory? Theory and Evidence from Payday Lending
nodes.summary: Develops a framework to evaluate payday lending regulation with behavioral consumers. Uses a within-subject experiment to measure biased beliefs about loan rollovers. Finds meaningful internalities from over-optimism about repayment. Optimal policy depends on whether the goal is correcting biases or reducing prices.

nodes.label: Overconfident Consumers in the Marketplace
nodes.summary: ★ STARRED. Reviews the literature on overconfident consumers in product markets. Firms exploit consumer overconfidence through shrouded add-on fees, unexpected charges, and complex pricing. Market competition does not eliminate exploitation. Policy interventions (disclosure, mandated simplicity) can improve welfare.

nodes.label: Heterogeneity, Demand for Insurance, and Adverse Selection
nodes.summary: Studies adverse selection when consumers have heterogeneous beliefs and risk preferences. Distinguishes between "type" variation (risk aversion, risk level) and "mistake" variation (biased beliefs about risk). Shows that corrective insurance subsidies can be welfare-improving when biased beliefs drive selection.

nodes.label: What Does a Deductible Do? The Impact of Cost-Sharing on Health Care Prices, Quantities, and Spending Dynamics
nodes.summary: Studies a large employer-mandated shift to high-deductible health plans using administrative claims. Finds consumers reduce spending bluntly across all care categories — including high-value preventive care — rather than targeting low-value spending. Implies that HDHPs impose welfare costs by inducing consumers to forgo valuable care, not just wasteful care.

nodes.label: Consumer Spending during Unemployment: Positive and Normative Implications
nodes.summary: Uses bank account transaction data to document that consumer spending drops sharply at UI benefit exhaustion — beyond what liquidity constraints alone predict. The pattern is consistent with present bias or reference dependence around the benefit level. Normative implication: optimal UI should taper benefits more gradually to smooth consumption over the unemployment spell.

nodes.label: Job Displacement Insurance and (the Lack of) Consumption-Smoothing
nodes.summary: Uses Brazilian administrative data to show that displaced workers experience large consumption drops despite generous severance pay and UI benefits. Workers spend most severance immediately rather than spreading it over the unemployment spell. Provides evidence that liquidity constraints and present bias jointly undermine consumption smoothing after job loss.

nodes.label: Unemployment Insurance and Job Search Behavior
nodes.summary: Uses French job-board data linked to UI records to study how UI generosity affects search effort and match quality. Finds that UI reduces search intensity but increases the quality of job applications and accepted offers. Overall welfare effect is positive: the option value of better matching outweighs the moral hazard cost of reduced search effort.

nodes.label: Job Seekers' Perceptions and Employment Prospects: Heterogeneity, Duration Dependence, and Bias
nodes.summary: Measures job seekers' subjective beliefs about reemployment using survey data and compares them to realized outcomes. Documents systematic overoptimism, especially among long-term unemployed. Beliefs update negatively with duration in ways inconsistent with Bayesian updating. Implications: correcting biased beliefs could improve search efficiency; optimal UI must account for heterogeneous and biased agents.

nodes.label: Evolving Choice Inconsistencies in Choice of Prescription Drug Insurance
nodes.summary: Extends the 2011 Medicare Part D analysis to examine how choice quality evolves as enrollees gain experience. Finds that choice inconsistencies persist and inertia is the dominant driver of suboptimal plan selection over time. Policies mandating active re-enrollment significantly improve welfare by forcing annual reconsideration.

nodes.label: The Nature of Risk Preferences: Evidence from Insurance Choices
nodes.summary: Estimates structural risk preferences from household deductible choices across home and auto insurance lines. Finds that probability distortions — overweighting small loss probabilities, as in prospect theory — are more important than diminishing marginal utility in explaining observed choices. Heterogeneity in probability weighting is substantial and policy-relevant.

nodes.label: Sources of Advantageous Selection: Evidence from the Medigap Insurance Market
nodes.summary: Documents advantageous selection in Medigap: healthier individuals buy more supplemental insurance, opposite to adverse selection predictions. Cognitive ability is the key omitted variable — high-ability individuals are both healthier and more likely to purchase supplemental coverage. Shows that multi-dimensional heterogeneity can reverse the direction of selection in insurance markets.

nodes.label: Private Information and Insurance Rejections
nodes.summary: Shows that private information about health risk causes large-scale insurance market unraveling: applicants who are rejected for coverage are precisely those with the most private knowledge of their high risk. Develops an empirical test for private information using rejection rates and subsequent mortality. Quantifies the welfare cost of private information through market exclusion.

nodes.label: Knowledge of Future Job Loss and Implications for Unemployment Insurance
nodes.summary: Estimates the degree to which workers have private information about their future job loss risk using expenditure and income data. Finds substantial private information that generates adverse selection in UI. Derives upper and lower bounds on the optimal UI replacement rate accounting for this selection, showing that optimal UI may be significantly lower than Baily-Chetty when private information is severe.

nodes.label: A Macroeconomic Approach to Optimal Unemployment Insurance: Theory
nodes.summary: Extends the Baily-Chetty optimal UI formula to a macroeconomic model with matching frictions. Adds a job-creation externality: UI raises workers' outside options, stimulating job creation by firms. In slack labor markets, the optimal replacement rate exceeds the partial-equilibrium optimum. Provides a new sufficient statistic for optimal UI that depends on the labor market tightness.

nodes.label: The Value of Unemployment Insurance
nodes.summary: Develops a revealed preference approach to measure the welfare value of UI using consumption and asset data. Constructs a sufficient statistic for the marginal value of UI that accounts for heterogeneity in liquidity constraints and risk preferences across workers. Finds the welfare value of UI substantially exceeds its fiscal cost for most worker types, justifying current generosity.

nodes.label: (Over)insuring Modest Risks
nodes.summary: Documents that homeowners systematically choose low deductibles for home insurance despite actuarially unfavorable premium-deductible trade-offs. The implied risk aversion required to rationalize choices is implausibly high (coefficients of relative risk aversion > 100). More plausible explanations include loss aversion and probability overweighting of modest, predictable losses.

nodes.label: Do Consumers Respond to Marginal or Average Price? Evidence from Nonlinear Electricity Pricing
nodes.summary: Exploits discontinuities in tiered electricity pricing to test whether consumers respond to marginal or average price. Finds strong evidence of average-price responses: consumers appear to pay their average rate, not the marginal rate they face on the next unit. This systematic misperception of nonlinear pricing implies large welfare losses and has direct implications for the design of environmental taxes and utility rate structures.

nodes.label: Smoke Gets in Your Eyes: Cigarette Tax Salience and Regressivity
nodes.summary: Studies differential salience of cigarette excise taxes (included in shelf price) vs. sales taxes (added at register) across income groups. Low-income smokers are more responsive to the salient excise tax than the non-salient sales tax; high-income smokers respond similarly to both. Tax salience varies by socioeconomic status, affecting both the behavioral response and the distributional incidence of cigarette taxes.

nodes.label: A Simple Mapping from MPCs to MPXs
nodes.summary: Derives analytical mappings from marginal propensities to consume out of income (MPCs) to marginal propensities to spend out of illiquid wealth (MPXs) in a model with present bias and illiquid retirement assets. Shows that present bias amplifies the household balance-sheet channels of fiscal and monetary policy. Provides micro-foundations for the high MPCs documented in household data.

nodes.label: How Do Individuals Repay Their Debt? The Balance-Matching Heuristic
nodes.summary: Analyzes credit card repayment behavior for millions of UK accounts. Documents that consumers use a balance-matching heuristic — splitting payments proportionally to card balances rather than directing payments to the highest-interest card. This simple rule is normatively sub-optimal (costing hundreds of dollars per year) but highly robust across consumer types and credit market conditions.

nodes.label: Borrowing to Save? The Impact of Automatic Enrollment on Debt
nodes.summary: Tests whether automatic 401(k) enrollment causes liquidity-constrained workers to substitute retirement saving for consumer debt. Using military personnel data, finds that auto-enrollment increases retirement savings without significant increases in non-retirement debt. Workers do not simply borrow to offset forced saving — the default raises net wealth, supporting the welfare case for nudge-based retirement policy.

nodes.label: Behavioral Industrial Organization
nodes.summary: Comprehensive handbook chapter reviewing how consumer biases shape firm strategy and market equilibrium. Covers shrouded add-on pricing (firms hide true costs), naivete about future usage (cell phones, credit cards), and switching costs with present-biased consumers. Shows that market competition does not protect naive consumers — firms can extract more surplus from biased consumers than from rational ones. Reviews policy interventions including disclosure mandates and fee regulation.

nodes.label: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
nodes.summary: Studies how default contribution rates in Danish retirement plans shape saving dynamics over the long run. Finds that defaults have large persistent effects due to inertia, but workers do eventually adjust — the "bite" of the default fades over time. Derives optimal dynamic defaults that front-load nudge strength early in workers' careers, yielding substantial welfare gains relative to static default policies.
